facts: Claude Code is described as an agentic coding tool that can read code, edit files, run commands, and integrate with development tools.
The official overview lists terminal, IDE, desktop, and web surfaces.
The overview describes CLI piping/scripting and custom workflows through the Agent SDK.

sources.title: Run Claude Code programmatically
sources.retrieval: functions.read canonical URL; reader returned the official Markdown alternate
sources.versionEvidence: 页面未声明版本号或 commit；页面示例包含版本条件时仅按页面原文读取，不将其转成项目版本
readFields: claude -p non-interactive invocation
allowedTools and permission modes
text/json/stream-json output formats
exit status and failure behavior
continue/resume and SIGTERM behavior
background-task and piped-stdin notes
facts: The Agent SDK can drive Claude Code programmatically through CLI, Python, or TypeScript.
claude -p runs non-interactively and can be combined with options such as --continue, --allowedTools, and --output-format.
The documented output formats are text, json, and stream-json; JSON can include session metadata and structured output.
Claude Code exits with code 0 on success and a non-zero code when the run fails; failures inside a run are printed as the result on stdout according to the page.
SIGTERM leaves the current turn unfinished and records no result for that turn; the page describes later resume behavior.
inferences: A CLI host can treat exit status, final result, and stream completion as separate observable signals.
Tool authorization, process signals, and output capture are host-facing integration concerns even when the Agent loop is supplied by a library or subprocess.
limitations: The page describes Claude Code-specific CLI semantics.
It does not establish exactly-once external effects, cross-process durable jobs, or this project's cancellation contract.
No real Provider or Model was run for R1.

facts: The Agent SDK is described as a library that runs the agent loop in the host process in Python or TypeScript.
The page distinguishes the SDK from the terminal-oriented CLI, direct Client SDK, and hosted Managed Agents.
The listed capabilities include tools, hooks, subagents, MCP, permissions, sessions, human-in-the-loop, and tracing.
Sessions are described as maintaining context across exchanges and supporting resume or fork.
inferences: An embedded host and a CLI host can consume different integration surfaces while sharing a conceptual agent loop.
A Harness research boundary should distinguish run-loop responsibilities from host permissions, products, and deployment.
limitations: The page describes Anthropic products and terms, not this project's target contract.
It does not decide whether NeuroAgentHarness should wrap a CLI, expose a library, or support both first.

sources.retrieval: functions.read canonical URL; reader returned the official documentation HTML

readFields: Agent, sandbox agent, realtime agent, handoff, guardrail, tracing, and session primitives
agent loop and function-tool schema validation
lower-level package and custom-provider composition notes
facts: The TypeScript SDK presents Agents, sandbox agents, realtime agents, agents-as-tools/handoffs, guardrails, tracing, and sessions as primitives or capabilities.
The SDK agent loop invokes tools, sends results back to the LLM, and continues until the task is complete.
The documentation describes lower-level packages for custom provider wiring or specific integrations.
inferences: An embedded backend host may need to compose model, tools, guardrails, sessions, and tracing rather than only call a one-shot completion API.
A provider-neutral Harness could be evaluated at the loop/state boundary while provider wiring remains in an adapter.
limitations: This is OpenAI SDK documentation, not evidence that the same abstractions are required here.
The page does not prove production recovery, exactly-once effects, or a preferred host for NeuroAgentHarness.

sources.title: Sessions
sources.retrieval: functions.read canonical URL; reader returned the official documentation HTML
sources.versionEvidence: 页面未声明 SDK release version or commit；未推测
readFields: automatic history retrieval and persistence around Runner.run
MemorySession and OpenAIConversationsSession
RunState resume with the same Session
custom Session storage and CRUD helpers
facts: When a Session is supplied, the runner retrieves prior items before a run and persists new user input and assistant output after a run completes.
The same Session is kept when resuming an interrupted RunState.
MemorySession is process-local and is reset when the process exits.
The Session interface can be implemented with storage such as Redis, DynamoDB, SQLite, or another datastore.
The documented Session helpers include getItems, addItems, popItem, and clearSession.
inferences: A product host that promises persistence must distinguish process-local memory from durable storage and define restart behavior.
Session history access and Invocation resume are related but separable host-observable concerns.
limitations: The page documents one SDK's Session contract, not a required NeuroAgentHarness schema.
It does not define tenant authorization, retention, migration, or external side-effect idempotency.

sources.title: Results
sources.retrieval: functions.read canonical URL; reader returned the official documentation HTML
sources.versionEvidence: 页面未声明 SDK release version or commit；未推测
readFields: RunResult and StreamedRunResult
finalOutput, newItems, history, interruptions, state, and streaming completion
approval resume and cancellation distinctions
facts: Non-streaming and streaming runs expose result surfaces including finalOutput, newItems, interruptions, and state.
history is described as replay-ready next-turn input, while newItems carries richer agent/tool/handoff metadata.
Approval interruptions are resumed by resolving state and passing the same state back to run.
A streamed run can finish cleanup after cancellation while finalOutput remains unset when the turn did not finish.
inferences: A host's success observation cannot be reduced to final text; it may need terminal status, interruption state, rich items, and stream completion.
A persistent product should define which result surface is durable, user-visible, or audit-only.
limitations: The documented fields are SDK-specific and do not prescribe this project's public API.
The page does not establish an external delivery protocol or business transaction boundary.

facts: The page states that each text generation request is independent and stateless.
Multi-turn conversations can be implemented by providing prior user and assistant messages as input.
The example appends all previous response output items, including reasoning items, before the next request.
inferences: A product host must explicitly choose whether conversation state is held locally, by a Session abstraction, or by a provider-managed mechanism.

sources.title: Persistence
sources.retrieval: functions.read canonical URL; reader returned the official Markdown alternate
sources.versionEvidence: 页面未声明 library release version or commit；未推测
readFields: persistence use cases
checkpointer versus store distinction
Agent Server, MemorySaver restart limitation, and persistent backends
facts: Persistence is described as useful for continuing conversations, resuming interruptions, recovering failures, or remembering information across interactions.
Checkpointers persist thread graph-state snapshots for short-term memory, human-in-the-loop, time travel, and fault tolerance.
Stores persist application-defined data across threads for preferences, facts, and shared knowledge.
MemorySaver/InMemorySaver store checkpoints in RAM and lose them on process restart; the page recommends a persistent checkpointer for production.
inferences: A persistent product host should not collapse current-run recovery state and cross-session application memory into one unspecified bucket.
Restart behavior is an observable product property, not only a storage implementation detail.
limitations: This is LangGraph documentation and its graph terminology does not define this project's model.
It does not prove a particular backend, consistency level, migration policy, or external side-effect guarantee.

sources.title: Temporal Workflow
sources.retrieval: functions.read canonical URL; reader returned the official Markdown alternate
sources.versionEvidence: 页面未声明 SDK/server release version or commit；未推测
readFields: Workflow Definition, Type, and Execution
resilience and Event History replay
determinism and Activity boundary for external effects
facts: Temporal distinguishes Workflow Definition, Workflow Type, and Workflow Execution.
The documentation says Workflow Executions emit Commands and process Events recorded in Event History.
After infrastructure failure, Temporal can recreate workflow state from Event History and replay code to resume.
Workflow code must be deterministic during replay; API calls, database queries, LLM invocations, and file I/O belong in Activities whose results are recorded and reused during replay.
inferences: An embedded backend host with long-running work may need a durable workflow owner separate from an in-process Agent loop.
External effects and replay/retry semantics must be explicit; a Harness should not claim workflow durability merely because it can serialize a local run state.
limitations: Temporal is a separate workflow platform, not a dependency or target implementation for R1.
Its guarantees require its own server, worker, Activity, and determinism model; they cannot be inferred for this repository.
